app.name: First Stone
app.tagline: A companion for your first kidney stone
banner.text: Education only — not a diagnosis. Fever, can't keep fluids down, can't pee, or pain your medicine doesn't control: go to the ER.
lang.label: Language
start.title: Before we start
start.intro: This app is for adults in the first month after a first kidney stone diagnosis. It explains your scan report, helps you watch for danger signs while the stone passes, and gets you ready for your follow-up visit.
start.private: Everything stays on this device. No account, no tracking.
start.safetyHelp: Please answer every question. If any answer is yes, we'll tell you what to do first.
start.dxLabel: When were you diagnosed, or sent home from the ER?
start.dxHelp: Your day count starts here. You can change it later in Settings.
safety.feverNow: Do you have a fever right now (38.0 °C / 100.4 °F or higher), or shaking chills?
safety.pregnant: Are you pregnant, or could you be?
safety.solitary: Do you have only one working kidney?
safety.transplant: Have you had a kidney transplant?
safety.ckd: Do you have kidney disease (for example, reduced kidney function)?
esc.call.title: Call emergency services now
esc.call.body: Call {number}, or have someone take you to the nearest emergency department. Don't drive yourself.
esc.er.title: Go to the emergency department now
esc.er.body: These signs can mean a blocked kidney with infection, or another problem that needs care today. Go to the nearest emergency department. If you can't get there safely, call {number}.
esc.contact.title: Contact your clinician
esc.contact.body: Call your urologist, your primary care clinician, or the clinic that treated you, and tell them what you noticed. If you can't reach anyone and you're worried, go to the emergency department.
scope.title: This app wasn't designed for your situation
scope.body: Kidney stones in pregnancy, in children and teens, with one kidney, after a transplant, or with kidney disease need closer care than this app plans for. Contact your clinician about your stone now.
scope.limited: You can still read the education sections, but the danger-sign checks were not designed for you.
scope.banner: Your safety answers mean this app's checks weren't designed for you. Follow your clinician's instructions first.
rule.faint: Fainting, feeling like you might faint, or confusion is an emergency.
rule.infection: Fever or shaking chills with a kidney stone can mean infection behind a blockage. This needs urgent care.
rule.painUncontrolled: Pain that your prescribed medicine doesn't control needs to be checked today.
rule.vomiting: Vomiting again and again, or not being able to keep fluids down, needs care today.
rule.cantUrinate: Not being able to pass urine needs care today.
rule.feverNow: Fever or shaking chills with a kidney stone can mean infection behind a blockage. This needs urgent care.
rule.pregnant: Kidney stones during pregnancy need care from your own clinician.
rule.solitary: With only one working kidney, a blocking stone can affect all of your kidney function.
rule.transplant: After a kidney transplant, a stone needs your transplant team's input.
rule.ckd: With kidney disease, a stone needs closer follow-up from your clinician.
rule.minor: This app is built for adults. Children and teens with stones need care from their own clinician.
rule.fourWeeks: It has been about 4 weeks and your stone hasn't been confirmed as passed. Guidelines advise checking with your clinician about next steps, which may include imaging.
rule.persist: Your discharge instructions said to get rechecked if symptoms last more than {hours} hours, and you're still having symptoms.
today.title: Today
today.noStone: Add the size and location from your scan report to see what published studies found.
today.passedOn: You marked your stone as passed on {date}.
today.passedUnsure: You think your stone passed on {date}, but you're not sure.
today.passedBtn: I think I passed my stone
today.lastCheckin: Your last check-in ({date}) had danger signs.
today.noFlags: No danger signs in today's check-in. Keep watching for them. Your clinician's instructions come first.
today.window: Guideline-based medicine to help passage is usually given for about {days} days.
today.summaryBtn: Print a summary for your visit
today.memoryWarn: This browser isn't saving data (private mode?). Your entries will be lost when you close it. Use Settings → Download backup to keep them.
checkin.title: Daily check-in
checkin.intro: About 30 seconds. Answer for how you feel right now.
checkin.flagsTitle: Do you have any of these?
checkin.painUncontrolled: Pain my prescribed medicine doesn't control
checkin.vomiting: Vomiting again and again, or can't keep fluids down
checkin.stoneSeen: I saw or caught a stone
checkin.resultNone: No danger signs in this check-in. Keep watching, and check in again if anything changes.
checkin.stoneSeenNext: You saw a stone — record it on the passed-stone page.
log.title: Your log
stone.title: My stone
stone.intro: Copy these from your CT scan report. If you don't have it, ask the ER or your clinic for a copy.
stone.sizeHelp: Use the largest number in the report. If it's in cm, multiply by 10: 0.5 cm = 5 mm.
stone.locHelp: The ureter is the tube between the kidney and the bladder. Reports may say "proximal" (upper), "mid", "distal" (lower), or "UVJ".
stone.met: Are you taking tamsulosin (Flomax) or another alpha-blocker for the stone?
stone.invalid: Enter a size between {min} and {max} mm.
loc.uvj: Where the ureter meets the bladder (UVJ)
ex.pass.likely: Most stones this size pass on their own.
ex.pass.mixed: Some stones this size pass on their own, but many need help from a urologist.
ex.pass.unlikely: Stones this size often need a procedure, though some still pass on their own.
ex.pass.kidney: This stone is still in the kidney, not on its way out. Some kidney stones are just watched and some are treated. Ask your clinician which applies to you.
ex.where.low: It's low down, near the bladder, which is where stones pass most often.
ex.where.high: It's higher up the ureter, where stones pass a bit less often than lower down.
ex.time.typical: It usually takes about {typ}, and sometimes up to {max}.
ex.time.big: For a stone this size, ask your clinician what to expect and when you'd decide about a procedure.
ex.metEffect.small: For stones this small, tamsulosin doesn't seem to make much difference.
ex.metEffect.larger: For stones this size, tamsulosin may help it pass, about {days} days sooner on average.
ex.do.strain: Pee through a strainer and keep any stone you catch. Bring it to your follow-up.
ex.do.checkin: Check in once a day. The app will tell you if anything needs care.
ex.do.fourWeeks: If it hasn't clearly passed in about 4 weeks, check back with your clinician.
ex.population: Based on studies of people with stones like this. Not a prediction for you.
ex.sizeRange: In the studies below, {low}–{high}% of stones this size passed on their own.
ex.sizeSingle: In the studies below, about {pct}% of stones this size passed on their own.
ex.collRow: {band} stones: {pct}% passed on their own. CT study of {n} people; size measured on axial CT images.
ex.jendRow: {band} wide stones: {pct}% passed within {weeks} weeks. CT study of {n} people; stone width measured.
ex.locationRow: Stones in this location: {pct}% passed on their own.
ex.unknownLoc: Location matters too. In one CT study, {p}% of stones in the upper ureter passed on their own, compared with {u}% where the ureter meets the bladder.
ex.kidney: The passage studies here looked at stones in the ureter. Stones sitting in the kidney are handled differently: some are watched, some are treated. Ask your clinician which applies to you.
ex.timing: In a study of {n} people, stones in the {band} range took {mean} days on average to pass. Of those that passed, 95% did so within {p95} days. {intervention}% of people in this group needed a procedure.
ex.timingOut: The time-to-passage study didn't include stones larger than 6 mm.
ex.timingNoMet: People in this 1999 study were not taking tamsulosin.
ex.metTitle: Medicine to help the stone pass
ex.met.strong: For stones in the lower ureter that are {mm} mm or smaller, the 2026 AUA surgical guideline strongly recommends that clinicians offer an alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin for about {days} days.
ex.met.conditional: For stones in the upper or middle ureter that are {mm} mm or smaller, the 2026 AUA surgical guideline says clinicians may offer an alpha-blocker. The evidence is weaker for these locations.
ex.met.overMax: The guideline's statements about medicine to help passage cover stones up to {mm} mm. Ask your clinician about next steps for a larger stone.
ex.met.notUreteral: Medicine to help passage has been studied for stones already in the ureter, not stones sitting in the kidney.
ex.met.locationUnknown: Guideline advice about medicine depends on where the stone is. Check the location in your report.
ex.metTrials: Trials disagree about how much it helps. In a large UK trial, about 80% of people didn't need a procedure whether they took tamsulosin or a placebo. In a US emergency department trial of mostly small stones, 50% passed with tamsulosin and 47% with placebo. A review of 55 trials found the benefit was mainly in larger stones.
ex.metYou: You said you're taking an alpha-blocker.
ex.metDecision: Whether you take it is a decision for you and your clinician. Don't start or stop any medicine because of this app.
ex.limit0: The short answer sorts these studies into three plain groups: most pass, some pass, often need a procedure.
ex.limit1: Studies measured stones differently (length or width, different CT views), so the same stone can fall into different size groups.
ex.limit2: They don't know about swelling, infection, how blocked your kidney is, or your anatomy.
ex.limit3: They followed people for different lengths of time (4 to 20 weeks).
ex.limit4: Where groups overlap, we chose the edges: for example, a stone of exactly 7 mm is placed in the 7–9 mm group.
ex.confirm: If it isn't clear that the stone has passed, guidelines advise confirming with imaging. Keep any stone you catch so it can be analyzed.
passed.title: Passing your stone
passed.strain1: Pee through a strainer: one from your clinic, a fine-mesh tea strainer, or a coffee filter.
passed.strain2: Let the stone dry. Keep it in a clean, dry container, not wrapped in tissue, where it can get lost.
passed.strain3: Bring it to your follow-up visit. Stone analysis shows what it's made of, which decides which prevention plan fits you.
passed.sureNo: I think so, but I'm not sure
passed.note: Passing one stone doesn't always mean every stone is gone. Ask whether you need imaging to confirm.
visit.title: Visit prep
visit.intro: Take these to your follow-up with a urologist or primary care clinician. Questions are added based on what you entered. Untick any you don't need.
visit.emphasis: Worth asking: you ticked a risk factor below.
visit.hrTitle: Am I at higher risk of more stones?
visit.hrIntro: European guidelines list conditions that make more stones more likely. Tick any that apply. This isn't a diagnosis — it's a list to discuss with your clinician.

visit.hrAny.one: You ticked 1 item. Ask whether a 24-hour urine test is right for you.
visit.hrAny.other: You ticked {n} items. Ask whether a 24-hour urine test is right for you.

visit.hrNone: Even without these, guidelines say first-time stone formers who are interested can be offered a 24-hour urine test.
visit.knowTitle: Good to know before your visit
hr.youngOnset: My first stone was as a child or teenager
hr.familyHistory: A parent, brother, or sister has had kidney stones
hr.stoneType: I've been told my stone is uric acid, brushite, or an infection stone
hr.solitary: I have only one working kidney
hr.metabolic: I have metabolic syndrome (for example, diabetes, obesity, and high blood pressure together)
hr.bowel: I have a bowel condition (like Crohn's disease), long-term diarrhea, or had weight-loss surgery
hr.genetic: I have a genetic condition linked to stones (like cystinuria)
hr.anatomy: I've been told my kidney or ureter has an unusual shape or a narrowing
know.fluid: To prevent new stones, guidelines aim for at least {l} liters of urine a day. That usually means drinking more than {l} liters. Ask what target fits you.
know.calcium: Don't cut calcium from food on your own. In a 5-year trial, a normal-calcium diet with less salt and less animal protein led to about half as many new stones as a low-calcium diet.
know.oxalate: Cutting out spinach, nuts, or other high-oxalate foods only matters for some people. Stone analysis and a 24-hour urine test show whether it applies to you.
know.tracking: A large 2026 trial found that coaching, smart water bottles, and cash rewards raised urine volume a little but didn't prevent new stones. A simple target and follow-up testing matter more than tracking every sip.
q.analysis: Can my stone be analyzed? If I catch it, where should I bring it?
q.highRisk: Am I at high risk of forming more stones?
q.urine24: Should I do a 24-hour urine test?
q.imaging: Do I need imaging to confirm the stone has passed and no others remain?
q.metConsider: Would a medicine like tamsulosin help me pass this stone?
q.metDuration: How long should I take the alpha-blocker, and which side effects should I watch for?
q.options: If it doesn't pass, what are my options (such as ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy), and when would we decide?
q.stent: When will my stent come out? Which symptoms are expected, and which are warning signs?
q.kidney: Does the stone in my kidney need treatment, or can we watch it?
q.fluid: How much should I drink each day, and how can I check my urine volume?
q.diet: Which diet changes apply to me? Do I need to limit oxalate?
q.pain: What should I do if the pain comes back?
q.redFlags: I had danger signs on {dates}. What does that change about my follow-up?
sum.title: Visit summary
sum.generated: Created {date} with First Stone. Patient-entered information for education only; not a diagnosis.
sum.stoneSection: Stone details (copied by the patient from their report)
sum.evidence: Figures shown to the patient come from published cohorts (see the app's evidence page, version {version}).
ev.title: Evidence & sources
ev.intro: Every number in this app comes from a published study or guideline, summarized in our own words. Numbers describe groups of people, not you.
ev.auaNote: The 2026 AUA guideline points are summarized from AUA announcements and abstracts. The full text requires a login, and statement numbers may change.
ev.rulesIntro: The checks are simple fixed rules, not AI. They can only tell you to get care; they never tell you that you're fine or can skip care. The rules file is open source so anyone can check it or report a mistake.
ev.linksNote: We link to these instead of copying them.
evf.collSize: In a CT study of 172 people with stones in the ureter, stones passed on their own in {s1}% at 1 mm, {s2}% at 2–4 mm, {s3}% at 5–7 mm, {s4}% at 7–9 mm, and {s5}% over 9 mm.
evf.collLoc: By location in the same study: {p}% in the upper ureter, {m}% in the middle, {d}% in the lower ureter, and {u}% where the ureter meets the bladder.
evf.jend: In a CT study of 392 people that measured stone width, stones passed within 20 weeks in {a}% at up to 3 mm, {b}% at 4 mm, {c}% at 5 mm, {d}% at 6 mm, and {e}% at 6.5 mm or wider.
evf.miller: In 75 people followed until their stone passed, it took {m1} days on average for stones 2 mm or smaller, {m2} days for 2–4 mm, and {m3} days for 4–6 mm. 95% of the stones that passed did so within {p1}, {p2}, and {p3} days.
evf.millerInt: In the same study, about {pct}% of stones larger than 5 mm needed a procedure.
evf.metAua: 2026 AUA surgical guideline: clinicians should offer an alpha-blocker for about {days} days for lower-ureter stones {mm} mm or smaller (strong recommendation); may offer it for middle and upper-ureter stones {mm} mm or smaller (conditional); and should confirm passage with imaging when it is uncertain.
evf.suspend: SUSPEND trial (1,167 UK adults): tamsulosin and nifedipine did no better than placebo. About {pct}% in each group needed no further procedure within 4 weeks.
evf.stoneTrial: US emergency department trial (512 adults, average stone {mm} mm): {t}% passed their stone within 28 days with tamsulosin and {p}% with placebo, a difference that could be due to chance.
evf.meta: A review of 55 trials found alpha-blockers made passage about {rr} times as likely overall, with the benefit concentrated in larger stones.
evf.metaTime: In the same review, alpha-blockers shortened the time to passage by about {days} days on average. For smaller stones (about {mm} mm or less) there was no clear benefit.
evf.infection: A blocking stone with signs of infection needs urgent drainage (2026 AUA surgical guideline, strong recommendation). European guidelines also advise fast-tracking people with fever, a single kidney, or an unclear diagnosis.
evf.returnSigns: Hospital and guideline patient leaflets agree: go back for fever, pain your medicine doesn't control, repeated vomiting, not being able to urinate, or fainting. Fever cut-offs differ, so we use the lower one: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F).
evf.revisit: In California, {pct}% of people sent home from emergency care with a kidney stone had another emergency visit for it within 30 days.
evf.roks: Among 2,239 first-time stone formers in Minnesota, a second symptomatic stone happened in {y2}% by 2 years, {y5}% by 5 years, {y10}% by 10 years, and {y15}% by 15 years. Predicted 10-year risk ranged from {lo}% to {hi}% depending on risk factors.
evf.roksValid: When the ROKS risk tool was tested in another group of patients, it separated higher and lower risk only modestly (AUC {auc2} at 2 years, {auc5} at 5 years). That's why this app doesn't give you a personal recurrence number.
evf.fluidTarget: AUA (2014 and 2026) and European guidelines aim for at least {l} liters of urine a day for most stone formers.
evf.borghiFluid: In a 5-year trial of people after a first calcium stone, {a}% of those who drank more water had another stone, compared with {b}% of those who didn't change.
evf.push: PUSH trial (1,658 people, 2026): coaching, a smart water bottle, and financial rewards raised urine volume modestly, but stone events were similar: {a}% with the program and {b}% without.
evf.borghiDiet: In 120 men with repeat calcium oxalate stones, a normal-calcium diet with less salt and animal protein led to about half as many new stones as a low-calcium diet ({a} vs {b} of 60 men over 5 years).
evf.auaDiet: AUA 2014: keep sodium to about 2,300 mg a day, get 1,000–1,200 mg of calcium a day from food, and limit high-oxalate foods only if urine oxalate is high.
evf.analysis: European guidelines advise stone analysis for everyone with a first stone, and further testing for those at high risk.
evf.urine24: AUA guidelines: offer a 24-hour urine test to first-time stone formers who are high-risk or interested.
evf.edInstr: In a survey of 99 emergency department stone patients in Lebanon, {a}% got no advice on preventing stones, yet {b}% wanted it.
evf.apps: A review of {n} popular water-tracking apps found none measured urine output or color, and only one explained urinary conditions linked to low fluid intake.

more.title: More
set.title: Settings & privacy
set.banner: Show the safety reminder at the top
set.bannerHelp: Danger-sign alerts from your check-ins still appear either way.
set.emergencyHelp: Shown in the danger-sign banner. For example: 911 (US), 119 (Korea), 112 (EU), 999 (UK).
set.persist: Re-check window from your discharge instructions (hours)
set.persistHelp: Optional. Some ERs say to come back if symptoms last more than, for example, 48 hours. Leave blank if yours didn't.
set.privacy: Everything you enter stays in this browser on this device. Nothing is sent anywhere: no accounts, analytics, cookies, or tracking. Because no health data leaves your device, it isn't held by a healthcare provider and isn't covered by HIPAA. Clearing your browser data erases it, so download a backup if you want to keep it.
set.passphraseHelp: At least 8 characters. There is no way to recover it if you forget it.
set.importAsk: This backup is encrypted. Enter its passphrase.
set.wrongPass: Wrong passphrase, or the file is damaged.
set.importConfirm: Restoring replaces everything currently stored in this app. Continue?
set.deleteConfirm: Delete all your data from this device? This can't be undone.
set.aboutText: First Stone is an open-source educational tool from robbiemed. It isn't a medical device. It doesn't diagnose, treat, or tell you what to do about medicines.
